Background Inflammation is considered a hallmark of concussion pathophysiology in experimental models, yet is understudied in human injury. Despite the growing use of blood biomarkers in concussion, inflammatory biomarkers have not been well characterized. Furthermore, it is unclear if the systemic inflammatory response to concussion differs from that of musculoskeletal injury. The purpose of this paper was to characterize systemic inflammation after injury in athletes with sport-related concussion or musculoskeletal injury. Methods A prospective, observational cohort study was conducted employing 175 interuniversity athletes (sport-related concussion, n = 43; musculoskeletal injury, n = 30; healthy, n = 102) from 12 sports at a sports medicine clinic at an academic institution. High-sensitivity immunoassay was used to evaluate 20 inflammatory biomarkers in the peripheral blood of athletes within 7 days of injury (subacute) and at medical clearance. Healthy athletes were sampled prior to the start of their competitive season. Partial least squares regression analyses were used to identify salient biomarker contributions to class separation between injured and healthy athletes, as well as to evaluate the relationship between biomarkers and days to recovery in injured athletes. Results In the subacute period after injury, compared to healthy athletes, athletes with sport-related concussion had higher levels of the chemokines’ monocyte chemoattractant protein-4 ( p < 0.001) and macrophage inflammatory protein-1β ( p = 0.001); athletes with musculoskeletal injury had higher levels of thymus and activation-regulated chemokine ( p = 0.001). No significant differences in biomarker profiles were observed at medical clearance. Furthermore, concentrations of monocyte chemoattractant protein-1 ( p = 0.007) and monocyte chemoattractant protein-4 ( p < 0.001) at the subacute time point were positively correlated with days to recovery in athletes with sport-related concussion, while thymus and activation-regulated chemokine was ( p = 0.001) positively correlated with days to recovery in athletes with musculoskeletal injury. Conclusion Sport-related concussion is associated with perturbations to systemic inflammatory chemokines that differ from those observed in athletes with a musculoskeletal injury. These results support inflammation as an important facet of secondary injury after sport-related concussion that can be measured systemically in a human model of injury. Keywords Inflammation Concussion Chemokines Cytokines Biomarkers Canadian Institute of Military and Veterans Health Research Task 7 Hutchison Michael G. issue-copyright-statement © The Author(s) 2019 Introduction Sport-related concussion (SRC) is a traumatic brain injury (TBI) induced by biomechanical forces. It is considered a mild form of TBI since no abnormalities are identified on standard structural neuroimaging [ 1 ]. The injury can result in a constellation of symptoms relating to impaired cognition, balance, vision, physical and emotional health, and sleep disturbances [ 2 , 3 ]. Full symptom resolution varies from days to weeks [ 1 , 4 , 5 ], with a number of patients (~ 15%) experiencing prolonged symptoms that can last months to years after injury [ 1 ]. Historically, a fundamental lack of understanding of the biological sequelae following injury has impeded the clinical translation of treatment options for SRC. Recently, studies employing advanced neuroimaging and fluid biomarkers have enhanced our knowledge of the mechanistic underpinnings of SRC in humans. These investigations have yielded evidence to support acute and subacute structural and functional alterations in the brain, including changes to functional connectivity [ 6 – 8 ] and cerebral blood flow [ 7 , 9 ], axonal/neuronal injury [ 10 – 13 ], oxidative damage/stress [ 14 ], and inflammation [ 7 , 15 , 16 ]. In a number of cases, perturbations have also been identified at medical clearance [ 6 , 7 , 14 , 17 ], suggesting a possible disconnect between clinical and biological recovery. However, despite being a central and well-studied component of secondary injury in moderate and severe traumatic brain injury (TBI) [ 18 – 21 ], the involvement of inflammation in SRC, particularly in the acute and subacute phases after injury, is comparatively less well characterized [ 15 , 16 ]. Elucidating its role has important implications for characterizing the recovery process, as well as expanding potential therapeutic strategies. Blood biomarkers are useful tools to measure inflammatory perturbations across the injury severity spectrum of TBI [ 14 , 18 , 19 , 22 , 23 ], and due to their relatively non-invasive and cost-effective nature, allow for sampling in a large number of participants. While characterizing inflammation in the peripheral blood can help uncover the potential systemic consequences of brain injury [ 24 – 27 ], because of the significant gene expression overlap between the peripheral blood and the CNS [ 28 ], it may also be used to reveal the inflammatory status of the brain. In view of this, a small number of studies have shown that SRC results in perturbations to systemically measured inflammatory indices. For example, we recently found a relationship between decreased global connectivity and higher peripheral blood levels of the chemokines' monocyte chemoattractant protein (MCP)-1 and MCP-4 in athletes within the first week of concussion [ 7 ]. In addition, there is evidence that inflammatory gene expression in peripheral blood mononuclear cells is altered within 6 h and at 7 days post-injury [ 15 , 16 ], and there are recent preliminary findings of increased blood concentrations of brain-derived extracellular vesicles carrying tumor necrosis factor (TNF)-α and interleukin (IL)-8 in the days following SRC [ 29 ]. Yet, despite the promise of utilizing peripheral blood biomarkers of inflammation to study human brain injury, prototypical inflammatory correlates—cytokines and chemokines—have not been well characterized throughout recovery following SRC. Given the complex, pleiotropic nature of the immune response to injury, an attempt at representing the inflammatory response to SRC need be mindful of potential confounds. First, the immune response differs between males and females [ 30 ]. Second, athletes are often injured during physical activity; vigorous exercise has known effects on the peripheral inflammatory response [ 31 – 34 ]. Lastly, in an athletic population it is important to assess the inflammatory response to musculoskeletal (MSK) injury in order to determine whether perturbations seen after SRC are specific to head trauma, or represent a general inflammatory response to injury [ 35 – 39 ]. Hence, the purpose of this study was to characterize inflammatory cytokine and chemokine profiles in the peripheral blood of athletes after SRC or MSK injury, both within the first week after injury and at medical clearance. We hypothesized that SRC would be associated with a unique blood signature distinct from MSK injuries, with persistent alterations present at medical clearance.

extracted_data.document_summary: This study investigated systemic inflammatory biomarker profiles in the peripheral blood of interuniversity athletes following sport-related concussion (SRC) or musculoskeletal (MSK) injury, compared to healthy controls. It revealed distinct chemokine perturbations in the subacute period (within 7 days of injury) for SRC (MCP-1, MCP-4, MIP-1β) compared to MSK injury (TARC). Several of these markers (MCP-1, MCP-4 for SRC; TARC for MSK) were found to be positively correlated with longer recovery times, suggesting inflammation as an important facet of secondary injury after SRC that can be systemically measured.

treatment_details.therapy_type: Observational study of systemic inflammatory responses to Sport-Related Concussion (SRC) and Musculoskeletal (MSK) injuries.
treatment_details.dose_specificity: A prospective, observational cohort study enrolled 175 interuniversity athletes (43 SRC, 30 MSK injury, 102 healthy controls). Peripheral blood samples were collected within 7 days of injury (subacute period, median 4-5 days) and at medical clearance to return-to-play (median 5 days post-clearance). Healthy athletes were sampled pre-season. This study did not involve therapeutic intervention or dose comparisons, focusing instead on characterizing biomarker profiles in response to injury.

measured_effect.magnitude_quantification: Higher concentrations in athletes with sport-related concussion compared to healthy athletes (p < 0.001) during the subacute period. Concentrations were positively correlated with days to recovery/medical clearance (p < 0.001) in SRC athletes. Elevated levels were also observed in athletes with a history of concussion and were correlated with lower functional connectivity in the brain in the subacute period after SRC.

analyzed_biomarkers.core_biological_function: Monocytic chemokine, involved in mediating inflammatory responses and the chemoattraction and recruitment of monocytes and macrophages to sites of injury.
analyzed_biomarkers.relevant_activity_context: Subacute period (within 7 days) after Sport-Related Concussion (SRC), and in athletes with a history of concussion.
analyzed_biomarkers.performance_or_health_indicator: Serves as a specific systemic inflammatory marker for sport-related concussion, discriminating SRC from healthy athletes. Its elevated levels are associated with prolonged recovery duration, potentially indicating pathological signaling that impedes recovery, and are correlated with decreased functional connectivity in the brain after SRC.
analyzed_biomarkers.research_outlook: Future research should further characterize its specific role in concussion pathophysiology and its potential as a diagnostic or prognostic biomarker for SRC severity, recovery duration, and therapeutic targeting. Investigation into its role in impeding natural recovery and the mediating effect of prior concussion history on chronic inflammation is warranted.

measured_effect.magnitude_quantification: Higher concentrations (p = 0.001) in athletes with sport-related concussion compared to healthy athletes during the subacute period. Increases have also been observed acutely after moderate-to-severe TBI.

analyzed_biomarkers.core_biological_function: Chemokine involved in inflammatory responses, primarily through the chemoattraction and recruitment of macrophages, monocytes, neutrophils, and other immune cells.
analyzed_biomarkers.relevant_activity_context: Subacute period (within 7 days) after Sport-Related Concussion (SRC).
analyzed_biomarkers.performance_or_health_indicator: Elevated levels serve as a specific systemic inflammatory marker for sport-related concussion, discriminating SRC from healthy athletes and consistent with inflammatory processes observed after TBI. Its precise contribution to secondary injury and/or recovery in sport concussion remains to be fully defined.
analyzed_biomarkers.research_outlook: Further investigation is needed to explore its precise involvement in the pathophysiology and mechanisms of sport-related concussion, its potential as a diagnostic biomarker, and its contribution to secondary injury and recovery. Research into the mediating effect of prior concussion history on chronic inflammation is also warranted.

measured_effect.magnitude_quantification: Higher concentrations (p = 0.001) in athletes with musculoskeletal injury compared to healthy athletes during the subacute period. Concentrations were positively correlated with days to recovery (p = 0.001) in athletes with musculoskeletal injury.

analyzed_biomarkers.core_biological_function: T-cell chemokine involved in inflammation and immune responses, particularly in the chemoattraction and recruitment of T-cells and Th2 lymphocytes.
analyzed_biomarkers.relevant_activity_context: Subacute period (within 7 days) after Musculoskeletal (MSK) injury.
analyzed_biomarkers.performance_or_health_indicator: Serves as a specific systemic inflammatory marker for musculoskeletal injury, discriminating MSK injury from healthy athletes. Its elevated levels are associated with longer recovery duration for this type of injury, indicating an active inflammatory process.
analyzed_biomarkers.research_outlook: Future studies are needed to elucidate the pathophysiological role of TARC in musculoskeletal injury, its specific involvement in inflammation and repair processes, and its potential as a diagnostic and prognostic biomarker for recovery duration and outcome.

measured_effect.magnitude_quantification: Concentrations at the subacute time point were positively correlated with days to recovery/medical clearance (p = 0.007) in athletes with sport-related concussion. Elevated concentrations were also noted in male athletes with a history of concussion, and acutely after moderate-to-severe TBI, where they correlate with adverse outcomes and mortality.

analyzed_biomarkers.core_biological_function: Monocytic chemokine, involved in mediating inflammatory responses, promoting the chemoattraction and recruitment of monocytes and macrophages to sites of inflammation and injury, and affecting CNS cytokine expression profiles.
analyzed_biomarkers.relevant_activity_context: Subacute period (within 7 days) after Sport-Related Concussion (SRC), acute moderate-to-severe Traumatic Brain Injury (TBI), and in male athletes with a history of concussion.
analyzed_biomarkers.performance_or_health_indicator: Associated with longer recovery duration following sport-related concussion, potentially indicating severity or persistent inflammatory processes. It is implicated in pathological signaling that prolongs recovery, exacerbates damage to brain tissue after injury, and correlates with adverse outcomes and mortality in TBI.
analyzed_biomarkers.research_outlook: Further research is warranted to fully characterize its role in SRC recovery, concussion healing, and its potential as a prognostic or therapeutic target. Investigation into its role in impeding natural recovery and the mediating effect of prior concussion history on chronic inflammation is crucial.
